texts: mixed: the rule fires, but everything it creates is keyed to the stone alone rather than to the soaking, so two submersions of the same stone collapse into one growth and one bloom, and that single bloom is then placed inside both soakings. Make each submersion the explicit trigger occasion: "Whenever a tide-pool stone is submerged, salt-bloom grows on that stone." (your fourth sentence uses 'whenever' and does get a fresh event per occasion).
good. parses as a fireable rule over salt-bloom crusts, each crust getting its own faint smell of salt, with 'faint' and 'of salt' both carried.

mixed: nothing asserted is false, but the packets never become actual things (they are recorded only as a kind of packet) and the nesting is lost — the parse says the keeping happens in packets and the keeping happens in the store, not that the packets sit in the store. Split the two containers into their own clauses: "The salt-bloom is kept in waxed paper packets, and those packets are kept in the Cauldron Hall store."

mixed: the rule fires and every other atom is right, but the burning mire-essence is filed as the doer of the burning instead of the thing that burns, so a question like 'what burns when salt-bloom is added?' will not match it. Your wording is not the cause — it is already one finite clause per condition with explicit subjects — so keep it exactly as written, "Whenever a Keeper adds salt-bloom to mire-essence, that mire-essence burns slowly.", and have the parse redone rather than reworded.
